title: Defect 5: a money picture like $8*89.99 mixes blank and star fill. Warn, and how?
why: The manuals do not forbid this picture (F p. 80; J 02.05.05). The 1962 machine code has one count for the whole leading run and one star switch, so the run gets one fill. Our compiler turns the star switch on, so 1.23 prints as $***1.23, and the dollar sign does not move up to the digits. Today the program compiles with the words the 1962 manual describes, and it prints no message. The question is whether to warn, and how strongly.
built: Draft PR #185 (branch defect-5-proto, head e62e838) builds option A. CI is green and 1604 tests pass. Probe deck: MIX $8*89.99, MOVE EXT (1.23) TO MIX. Default listing: NO ERRORS WERE DETECTED DURING COMPILATION, then the run ends AT 5,00 STOP RUN. The run test reads MIX back as $***1.23.

opts.t: Keep the 1962 code; add our own note, shown only with --pedantic
opts.d: Default mode does not change: the program compiles and runs on the 1962 words. A user who asks for strict notes learns that the whole run fills with stars. The printed $***1.23 still differs from the manual's per-cell rules, where the 8 cell is blank and the dollar floats. To reverse it, remove one message, its check and its tests.
opts.pre: 3,00    1    LEADING RUN OF 'MIX' MIXES 8 AND *. ASTERISKS FILL IT. (NON-HISTORICAL.)

opts.t: Print the 1962 message 33 (illegal combination) in default mode
opts.d: The program still compiles and runs. But the listing calls the picture illegal, and no manual says that. Every such field in every program gets the message by default, so a later reader learns a rule that does not exist.
opts.pre:
3,00    1    ILLEGAL COMBINATION OF FORMAT CHARACTERS. CHECK DATA DESCRIPTION.
                    'MIX' FORMAT USED.

opts.t: Refuse to generate code
opts.d: A program the 1962 compiler would have compiled stops compiling here. That breaks your rule of 14 September. It also goes against your choice of 2 November on defects 1 to 11 ('generate the correct code wherever the manuals show the code'), and the manual shows the code for this picture. The listing says NO ERRORS, but nothing runs. Not built; the sample is illustrative.
opts.pre: error: job 1: unrecovered shape: an edited field whose leading run mixes 8 and * (RT-5)

recwhy: Two rules you already gave decide this. The 1962 compiler would compile this picture, so ours must. The manual shows the 1962 code for it, so we use that code and do not refuse. Option A follows both rules. It changes no default listing and does not invent an illegality. A user who wants the warning gets it.

title: A BEGIN SECTION with no name of its own: which message, if any?
why: The 1960 manual (F p. 26) says a section must start with its own name, then BEGIN SECTION. Today the first shape opens two sections, both named S1. The second opens a section with no name and prints no message. Code generation then stops on both with an internal error. No 1962 message names this case. If the 1962 compiler accepted these shapes, any 'illegal' message we print would be false. If it rejected them, compiling them is wrong. Your 14 September rule sends that call to you.
built: Draft PR #183 (branch nameless-begin-proto, head 861348f) builds the 196 option. The gate passes (1602 tests). The listings of all four fixture decks match master byte for byte. Parser tests cover both shapes. The code generator's 'unnamed section' stop could no longer be reached, so it was deleted. The 192 and 950 options are not built.

The mixed-verb rule already produces this same extra message today. The program compiles. Risk: if the 1962 compiler accepted these shapes, a real 1962 message now calls them illegal. Easy to change later.
opts.pre: Both shapes (built, checked): '   3,00    3    ILLEGAL SENTENCE STRUCTURE NOTHING DONE.' then '   5,00    3    CANNOT -END- SECTION WHEN NONE ARE OPEN.'

opts.t: Drop only the extra BEGIN with msg 192 and keep the rest of the sentence (D1.5 also uses 192 for a misused key word)

Shape 2 still draws msg 64 at the END. The parser has no code today that drops one clause and keeps the sentence. That code would need to be written. Not built.
opts.pre: Not built; from a throwaway patch, not checked. Shape 1: '   3,02    3    SENTENCE STRUCTURE ERROR. POSSIBLE ILLEGAL USE OF A KEY WORD.' Shape 2: the same text, then msg 64 at 5,00. The patch printed 3,00 for shape 2, but our clause-numbering rule (M2-6) suggests 3,01.

opts.pre: Not built; from a throwaway patch, not checked. Both shapes: '   3,00    3    BEGIN SECTION HAS NO NAME OF ITS OWN. NOTHING DONE. (NON-HISTORICAL.)' then msg 64 at 5,00.

opts.t: Accept both shapes with no message, on the view that the 1962 compiler accepted them
opts.d: Under your 14 September rule, this means generating code for them. That is our own design, because the 1962 sample shows no such code. Open problems: what END S1 and DO S1 mean when two sections share one name. Not built. Until it is, the compiler stops with an internal error, as it does today.
opts.pre: Today on master (checked). Shape 1: '   6,00    4    ONE OR MORE SECTIONS NOT CLOSED.' then 'error: job 1: unrecovered shape: a section beginning inside an open section (no sample instance)'. Shape 2: '  NO ERRORS WERE DETECTED DURING COMPILATION' then 'error: job 1: unrecovered shape: an unnamed section (no sample instance)'.

recwhy: F p. 26 says a section must have its own name, so the strongest evidence says 1962 rejected these shapes. 196 is a real 1962 message whose text says what happens. The parser already uses it to delete sentences that break a stated F rule (M2-12). It needs no new message id, and both shapes then compile. The risk named under 950 is real but weaker than F's 'must'.

title: Two PROGRAM.START labels: compile with the first, as D2.1 says, or keep refusing?
why: D2.1 says the first label wins and compilation goes on. Today the compiler prints the listing with both messages but produces no object deck. Your 2026-11-02 rulings point both ways. 'Handle defects wherever the manuals show the code' favours compiling, because the manual's message says FIRST USED. 'Compile means the listing; refusals stay' says today's refusal already meets your 2026-09-14 rule.
built: Draft PR #184 (branch d21-proto, head 72d922c, CI green, 1606 tests pass, golden files unchanged) builds the 'first' option. It contains the code change, a dated D2.1 amendment marked 'prototype for Jack's call', four tests and a machine run. The 'refuse' option is master as it stands, plus the amendment text below. That amendment is on no branch yet. Neither option is merged. The two texts that collide: - D2.1: "At most one PROGRAM.START is allowed per program (msg 141 'MORE THAN ONE -PROGRAM.START-. FIRST USED.' on a second occurrence, first one wins, compilation continues)". - The code generator's guard on a name defined twice: "a procedure name defined twice (no sample instance)". This guard serves section-scoped names in general (D2.5). It is not a PROGRAM.START rule. The 2026-09-06 record justified keeping it with M4-2, which refuses shapes no sample shows. But M4-2 limits that refusal to a shape that "no [J 90.04] message covers", and this shape draws two messages, 141 and 166. Refuse option, D2.1 amendment text for verbatim use: *Amended 2026-11-02.* The generator refuses a program with two PROGRAM.START labels. The refusal comes from the duplicate-name guard of the label binder (D2.5). It is not a PROGRAM.START rule. The parser still issues msg 141 of [J 90.04.01], and the resolver still issues msg 166, so the listing prints in full. No sample program shows object code for the path where compilation continues. The words "first one wins" above describe the 1962 processor, as the text of msg 141 ("FIRST USED") shows. They do not describe this generator.

opts.t: Compile it using the first label, as D2.1 says (PR #184)
opts.d: The program gets an object deck whose start address and every GO TO PROGRAM.START point at the first label. A machine test confirms it: NUM reads 1, which happens only when the run starts at the first label. The change adds no new kind of machine code. It only chooses which label the name means. No sample shows the result, so only the decision record can check it. Message 166 (severity 3, our own assignment because the manual prints none) still fires, so --run does not run the job, but the deck is punched. One case still refuses: a second label that opens a section, because its END would return to the wrong place. A DO into PROGRAM.START is already an error by itself (message 143). To undo it, revert the PR: two code changes, four tests and one amendment.
opts.pre:
3,00   71177 PROGRAM.START.  SET NUM = NUM + 1.
5,00   71200 PROGRAM.START.  SET NUM = 2.
5,00    1    MORE THAN ONE -PROGRAM.START-. FIRST USED.
5,00    3    'PROGRAM.START' IS NOT UNIQUE IN THIS SECTION.
SEVERITY LIMIT WAS NOT REACHED
job 1: not run: maximum severity 3

opts.t: Keep the refusal and add the amendment above to D2.1
opts.d: The listing prints with both messages, but no object deck is produced. Under your 2026-11-02 ruling that 'compile' means the listing, this already meets your 2026-09-14 rule. It claims less: no code without a sample behind it enters the M7 comparison with the 1963 compiler. Once the amendment lands, D2.1 no longer misleads a reader. The cost is a refusal that leans on M4-2 although two manual messages cover this shape. To undo it, remove one paragraph later.
opts.pre:
5,00    1    MORE THAN ONE -PROGRAM.START-. FIRST USED.
5,00    3    'PROGRAM.START' IS NOT UNIQUE IN THIS SECTION.
SEVERITY LIMIT WAS NOT REACHED
error: job 1: unrecovered shape: a procedure name defined twice (no sample instance)

recwhy: The deciding question is whether the manual's own message, "FIRST USED", counts as the manual showing what the 1962 compiler did. I think it does. It names the outcome exactly, and 'first' adds no new kind of machine code, only a choice of label. That fits your ruling to handle defects 'wherever the manuals show the code'. If only a sample listing counts as evidence, choose 'refuse': your listing ruling then covers it. The 2026-09-06 recommendation to refuse came before both 2026-11-02 rulings. If you take 'first', the 'prototype for Jack's call' tag comes off the D2.1 amendment before the merge.

title: W3: take “the compiler tags each line with its statement” forward as the real W3?
why: W3 needs the compiler to say which statement each line of each panel belongs to. The roadmap already asks for this to come from the compiler, because the site must hold no compiler knowledge (HANDOVER, 'The rule that keeps it cheap'). The other two ways each fail on a fact. Numbers written into the text would change four golden files and cannot go into the Cards or Listing panels at all. A site that works the numbers out itself breaks that rule, and it could match Code rows only through statement names.
built: Draft PR #189 (branch w3-design, head deab534; gate and CI green). To see it, run: dart run tool/build_web.dart; python3 -m http.server 8000 --directory web; then open localhost:8000. In the Listing tab, click the line `188,00 71466 START. OPEN ALL FILES,`. Its three lines turn yellow, and the tabs read Cards 3, Scan 1, Parse 11, Semantics 3, Listing 3, Code 19. In Code, the 19 rows from `00165 GN)000 START TSX SYS)175,4` to `00207 TRA END.OF.MASTERS+1` are marked. Click `188,03 get-clause` in Parse, then open Code: the six GET rows (00177 to 00204) show in darker yellow. The status line reads 'Statement 188,03 · 188 of 229', and the right arrow goes to 189. Not yet tagged: 412 of 619 Semantics lines (the storage, records and items rows, and most dictionary rows) and 169 of 970 Code lines (the data words, the shared constants and a few shared blocks).

opts.t: The compiler sends the numbers beside the text (built in PR #189)
opts.d: Adds one JSON key and no golden file. Each stage writer and the listing writer collect the numbers as they print, and the code generator records one field on each word. The site change is about 190 lines of JS, CSS and HTML. Which clause a code word belongs to is our own call: no 1962 printout says. Many Semantics and Code rows have no number yet (see 'built'). Easy to reverse, because no dump changes.

opts.t: Write the numbers into the text
opts.d: The Scan, Parse, Semantics and Code golden files all change. The Cards panel is the deck's own text file, and its format is frozen. The Listing must match the 1962 printout byte for byte. So neither of those two can take a number. The join would cover four panels of six, unless each dump gets a second, numbered copy.

opts.t: The site works out the numbers from the text
opts.d: The site must learn the column layout of each panel, which breaks the rule that the site holds no compiler knowledge. Any later change to a panel's text would quietly break the site. In Code, the site could match only statements that have a name, such as START. A statement with no name (189), or a single clause, has nothing to match. Cheapest to start, but every later milestone costs more.

recwhy: A is the only choice that keeps every golden file unchanged, reaches all six panels at the clause level, and needs no compiler knowledge in the site. The rows without a number are work still to add, and none of it needs a redesign. Data entries carry their own statement numbers (for example 36,00), so the data words and the untagged Semantics rows can take them later.

title: W4: the run button works in the browser. What form should the tutorial take?
why: Run works. The sample's two input tapes are built into the page (under 5 KB), so a run needs no download. Loading the tapes over the network gains nothing. Generating them in the browser would ship a test tool. Run uses the deck in the editor. Still open: where the tutorial lives. Jack asked for a tutorial page separate from the front page. The roadmap says that page uses the existing editor and no second one.
built: Draft PR #188 (branch w4-design, head a31994d, CI green). test/web_run_test.dart checks that the sample prints 'AT 199,14 STOP RUN' plus test/goldens/90.05-payroll.report, and tests a fault, the step budget, severity, a job with no object program and an empty deck. test/runtime/tape_store_test.dart holds both tape stores to one contract. test/layering_test.dart now requires that the browser import walk reaches machine.dart. `node tool/check_web_run.mjs` printed 'The WebAssembly run prints the report golden, in 63 ms.' In headless Chrome, Run selects the 07 Run tab and shows '71 lines · reached end of job · 17 ms'.

opts.t: A separate tutorial.html with the same bench markup and the same app.js
opts.d: The lessons sit beside the one editor, so a lesson can load a deck and press Run in place. One app.js means one set of card-column rules, which is the reason the roadmap gives for refusing a second editor. Cost: a second copy of about 100 lines of bench markup, plus a test that keeps the two copies the same. app.js also needs changes to start on either page, because today it fails on a page with no build stamp. Easy to undo.

opts.t: Tutorial sections around the bench on the front page
opts.d: No second copy of the markup. But Jack asked for a separate tutorial page, so this goes against his own request. The front page exists to bring a reader in, and web-copy rule A4 limits its paragraphs to three sentences. Eleven lessons would bury the compiler. Moving them out later means rewriting the page.

opts.t: A text-only tutorial page; each example is a share link that opens the front page with that deck
opts.d: Cheapest: no editor code, and share links already exist. The reader goes back and forth between two pages and loses 'change a line, run, see the report change' on one screen. It goes against the roadmap's 'the tutorial page, with the W1 editor', so that entry would need an edit.

opts.t: Scope alternative: a language course of many small programs instead of one walk through the sample
opts.d: Teaches more of COMTRAN. But any example that reads input needs its own input tapes built into the site. Each example also needs a test that keeps it compiling, or the tutorial breaks silently when the compiler changes. The writing and test cost is several times that of the walk through the sample.

recwhy: A is the only form that puts the lesson and the running program on one screen with one editor. Its one cost, a second copy of the markup, is caught by a cheap test. Keep the scope to one walk through the sample. Every lesson that uses the unedited sample can then be tied to the existing 90.05 goldens. That includes the defect-10 lesson: RET.PREM is read as INS.PREM (M6-4 finding 1). Lesson 8, where the reader edits a line, needs a test of its own.
